Before the answer returns, the network must solve several problems.

Which model can handle the task?

Which GPU is compatible?

Is the miner available?

Can it complete the request quickly?

Is the node reporting its condition honestly?

And should that operator be rewarded when the work is finished?

Imagine a user uploading a 70-page report and asking an application:

“Summarise the document, identify the major risks and prepare five recommendations.”

The application sends the request through an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint.

The developer does not need to own the GPU that will process it.

But the network cannot send the job to any connected machine.

One miner may host Qwen.

Another may run a different model.

A smaller GPU may lack enough memory.

A powerful node may already be overloaded.

The request must be matched with infrastructure capable of performing that specific workload.

A selected miner receives the prompt.

Its model runtime performs the inference.

The GPU reads the report and generates the requested output.

This is the useful work being purchased.

The miner does not create value merely by connecting expensive hardware.

It creates value by remaining available, accepting real jobs and producing reliable results.

But a returned answer does not automatically prove honest service.

A machine may be online while running the wrong model.

It may return incomplete output.

It may misreport performance.

It may accept workloads that exceed its capabilities.

BTTInferGrid’s miner architecture therefore includes more than the inference runtime.

A metrics exporter reports GPU conditions.

A miner agent manages identity, registration, signed heartbeats and challenge responses.

The control plane can observe whether the node remains ready.

If heartbeats disappear, the machine should not continue receiving jobs as though nothing happened.

Validators add another layer.

They can issue challenges designed to test miner behaviour.

The operator should not always know whether a request is an ordinary customer workload or an audit.

Predictable tests allow selective honesty.

Randomised checks make it harder for a miner to behave correctly only when it knows it is being examined.

Multiple validator assessments can contribute to a broader performance score.

One judge should not possess unlimited authority over a miner’s reputation.

Repeated reliable service can strengthen confidence.

Dishonest or unstable behaviour can reduce rewards or create penalties.

The final answer returns to the application.

The user receives the summary.

They may never know who operated the GPU.

That is the point.

Infrastructure should make complexity manageable, not force every user to inspect the machine behind every response.

One prompt has now travelled through:

API access.

Model matching.

Miner selection.

GPU inference.

Metrics.

Heartbeats.

Validation.

Performance scoring.

Response delivery.

Economic settlement.

BTTInferGrid is not merely a marketplace where GPU owners advertise hardware.

It is an attempt to transform scattered machines into measurable AI service.
